intent: a two-minute film for a luxury board: what a government offer labelled strategic costs the partner, told through the cases

through_line.title: The Cost of 'Strategic'
through_line.question: When a government stamps a deal 'strategic,' who actually pays—and do the partners get to choose?
through_line.face_on_the_stake: The junior partner (Australia locked into AUKUS delays; SeaMeWe-6 consortium members absorbing sanction risk; Greece surrendering land, law, and energy to Microsoft) who committed believing the label meant shared gain.

value_turn.before: Partners enter deals expecting mutual gain, sovereign capability, or strategic elevation.
value_turn.after: Partners discover they have subsidised the dominant power's industrial or geopolitical agenda while absorbing environmental, financial, and sovereign costs.
value_turn.turned_by: The moment of commitment—AUKUS signature, SeaMeWe-6 consortium vote, Greece's Strategic Investment approval—after which exit becomes prohibitively costly.

through_line.antagonism: Governments wield the word 'strategic' as a unilateral instrument—reclassifying land, threatening sanctions, engineering markets—while private and junior-state partners absorb costs they did not price and cannot reverse.
through_line.open_loop: Australia may end up with no sovereign submarine capability after generations of commitment; Greece's 300 jobs may never materialise; private consortium members who complied with US sanction pressure have no recourse for losses absorbed.
through_line.verdict_possible: Supported across four sources: in every case the 'strategic' label transfers risk and cost downward to the junior partner while concentrating upside with the dominant state or its preferred commercial coalition. A clear verdict is available.
through_line.why: All four carrying sources turn on the same structural irony: a government designates something 'strategic,' the designation imposes asymmetric costs on partners, and the partners have no ex-ante legal or political recourse. The fifth source (BDC/Canada) concerns domestic state VC and has no cross-border partner-cost dynamic, so it contextualises but does not carry this line.

approach.why: The story map supplies an explicit, cross-source verdict: 'in every case the strategic label transfers risk and cost downward to the junior partner while concentrating upside with the dominant state or its preferred commercial coalition.' The verdict is not speculative—it is documented across four case studies with quantified costs (AUD 4.1 bn, 159% energy load, 20% funding hole, 12 FTE vs. 300 promised) and a consistent structural mechanism. For a two-minute board film whose intent is 'what a government offer labelled strategic costs the partner, told through the cases,' the verdict card is the only structure that can carry that intent without sprawl: it opens on the word itself ('strategic'), walks through three rapid case exhibits, and closes with the verdict named once in the sources' own terms. The film gives away the structural irony at once—that is the hook—and holds back the quantified proof case by case. The face on the stake is the junior partner across all cases; the antagonist is the dominant state wielding the label. Runner-up is the_case, which would commit to one episode's reversals and lose the cross-case pattern the map explicitly needs.
approach.must_cut: The BDC/Canada line (up4E97C254) is a contextualiser, not a case carrier for the strategic-label-cost through-line, and must be cut or collapsed to a single number to protect the two-minute ceiling. The sovereignty-paradox sub-argument must be subordinated to the verdict structure rather than developed as its own arc.

movements.title: the mechanism
movements.job: Close the loop: name the structural finding once, plainly. The motif word 'strategic' returns alone on screen. The board is left with a question they can carry into their next deal.

value_turn.before: Boards and governments enter 'strategic' arrangements believing the label signals shared risk and shared gain
value_turn.after: The label is revealed as a one-way transfer; the film closes with three diagnostic questions the board can apply
value_turn.turned_by: up48EE8ED8:quotable:2 ('pathological symbiosis') and up737F3D26:reveal:1 (screening as coercion tool, not neutral protection)

movements.narration_hint: Three cases. One structure. The label transfers floor risk to the junior partner. Upside concentrates with the dominant power. 'Semi-peripheral countries like Greece are locked into a form of pathological symbiosis.' Australia. A cable consortium. Greece. The word was the same. So was the result. Before you sign: who bears the floor? Who captures the upside? What recourse exists if the benefit never arrives?

motif.what: The word 'strategic'—spoken by governments to justify AUKUS, SeaMeWe-6, and Greece 2.0; used as a legal instrument in investment screening. Planted as neutral, official-sounding designation; paid off as the mechanism of cost transfer.

hook.why: Six words from the source itself—'a geopolitical tool of empire'—delivered cold over black, no title card, no music. Intensity-5 element. The board hears the verdict before they know the evidence; the film then earns it across three cases. Maximum disruption in the first three seconds.

spine.open_loop: Every time a government stamps a deal 'strategic,' a junior partner absorbs costs they did not price—financial, sovereign, environmental. Three documented cases. One structural finding. Does your next deal carry this label?
spine.colour_script: Movements 1–4 live inside a cold, high-contrast palette: near-black backgrounds, steel-blue and slate midtones, single warm amber accent for the word 'strategic' each time it appears on screen. Phase 1 (cold authority): deep charcoal and slate, amber type accent #E8A020 against dark ground—the word lands with weight. Phase 2 (industrial pressure): steel-blue and gunmetal, slightly warmer as case evidence accumulates, type accent #C8D8E8 (pale cool) against the blue-grey footage of cable ships, construction sites, and factory floors. Phase 3 (cost revealed): the warmth drains; near-monochrome with a single red-orange accent #E05A20 on the cost numbers—emissions up 50%, 12 FTE, no sovereign submarine—so each number reads as an alarm. Phase 4 (verdict): full black ground, the amber of phase 1 returns on the controlling idea, closing on the motif word 'strategic' alone on screen, now stripped of comfort.
spine.musical_arc: Score enters under movement 2 as a low, held string tone—not melodic, just present, a constant tension beneath the case evidence. It does not resolve. Through movement 3 a higher, thinner string layer enters above the held note, creating dissonance as cost numbers accumulate. At the pivot into movement 4 both layers thin to silence; the verdict is spoken over nothing. A single piano chord—unresolved—closes on black. The board should feel the absence of resolution, not comfort.
spine.verdict: In every case the 'strategic' label transfers floor risk downward to the junior partner while concentrating upside with the dominant state or its preferred commercial coalition. The word is not a shared bet—it is a one-way transfer mechanism.
